I think Anthropic and OpenAI have found product-market fit

I think Anthropic and OpenAI have found product-market fit [ https://substack.com/redirect/1024b51f-17df-4502-b377-51795e2c02a0?j=eyJ1IjoiOGZ6aG43In0.MEdLiOcZRUc_N3oL6SgEUFCyFYN9tX8izo2S8jR1GNw ] - 2026-05-27
Anthropic are strongly rumored [ https://substack.com/redirect/f48674de-233d-4de5-85f5-bc6fc9f8596b?j=eyJ1IjoiOGZ6aG43In0.MEdLiOcZRUc_N3oL6SgEUFCyFYN9tX8izo2S8jR1GNw ] to be about to have their first profitable quarter. Stories are circulating [ https://substack.com/redirect/9e749f1a-e68f-407d-9329-e2772c15fc00?j=eyJ1IjoiOGZ6aG43In0.MEdLiOcZRUc_N3oL6SgEUFCyFYN9tX8izo2S8jR1GNw ] of companies surprised at how expensive their LLM bills are becoming from usage by their staff. I think this is because OpenAI and Anthropic have both found product-market fit.
Enterprise customers are now paying API prices [ https://substack.com/redirect/8b593aa7-455b-4f60-b700-a229feedd357?j=eyJ1IjoiOGZ6aG43In0.MEdLiOcZRUc_N3oL6SgEUFCyFYN9tX8izo2S8jR1GNw ]
I think they’ve found product-market fit [ https://substack.com/redirect/e40a9cea-fcd0-4499-8c92-1989cbc2d50e?j=eyJ1IjoiOGZ6aG43In0.MEdLiOcZRUc_N3oL6SgEUFCyFYN9tX8izo2S8jR1GNw ]
And they’re ramping up [ https://substack.com/redirect/0b7a20c5-5c3c-4325-ae10-5c23b820b532?j=eyJ1IjoiOGZ6aG43In0.MEdLiOcZRUc_N3oL6SgEUFCyFYN9tX8izo2S8jR1GNw ]
The AI-failure stories around this are pretty thin [ https://substack.com/redirect/927cde06-9f4b-43ad-b367-af810958d17b?j=eyJ1IjoiOGZ6aG43In0.MEdLiOcZRUc_N3oL6SgEUFCyFYN9tX8izo2S8jR1GNw ]
We also know the labs are spending a lot [ https://substack.com/redirect/43d81203-85d4-4d5b-9ea1-4ea0e282aca3?j=eyJ1IjoiOGZ6aG43In0.MEdLiOcZRUc_N3oL6SgEUFCyFYN9tX8izo2S8jR1GNw ]
API revenue is becoming less important [ https://substack.com/redirect/a9a4cf63-a4f2-4973-9c29-0e4ea0901c28?j=eyJ1IjoiOGZ6aG43In0.MEdLiOcZRUc_N3oL6SgEUFCyFYN9tX8izo2S8jR1GNw ]
April is a new inflection point [ https://substack.com/redirect/078d8706-7f19-43fb-810e-fa6a961c05a3?j=eyJ1IjoiOGZ6aG43In0.MEdLiOcZRUc_N3oL6SgEUFCyFYN9tX8izo2S8jR1GNw ]
Enterprise customers are now paying API prices
I currently subscribe to the $100/month Max plan from Anthropic and the $100/month Pro plan from OpenAI. If you are a heavy user of coding agents these plans are a fantastic deal. I just ran the ccusage [ https://substack.com/redirect/79c0d910-aa60-4671-894d-af602475b14d?j=eyJ1IjoiOGZ6aG43In0.MEdLiOcZRUc_N3oL6SgEUFCyFYN9tX8izo2S8jR1GNw ] tool on my laptop to get an estimate of how much I would have spent if I were to pay for API tokens in the past 30 days and got:
$1,199.79 for Anthropic Claude Code
$980.37 for OpenAI Codex
That’s $2,180.16 worth of tokens for $200 - not bad at all! I’m a moderately heavy user of these tools, but I’m certainly not running agents every hour of the day and night.
I had assumed that companies making extensive use of agents were getting similar discounts. It turns out I could not have been more wrong about that.
I haven’t been able to track down the exact date, but at some point in the last six months Anthropic switched their Enterprise plan (originally “Claude seats include enough usage for a typical workday” back in August 2025 [ https://substack.com/redirect/4114fe09-ec3e-4dc6-9f29-a0cf78f120e5?j=eyJ1IjoiOGZ6aG43In0.MEdLiOcZRUc_N3oL6SgEUFCyFYN9tX8izo2S8jR1GNw ]) to $20/seat/month plus API pricing for usage. This story about the change from The Information [ https://substack.com/redirect/0b99d7bb-1898-49f4-a5ec-05c0cce1e853?j=eyJ1IjoiOGZ6aG43In0.MEdLiOcZRUc_N3oL6SgEUFCyFYN9tX8izo2S8jR1GNw ] is dated Apr 14, 2026, but cites an Anthropic spokesperson claiming that the pricing change occurred in November 2025. Existing customers are finding out about the change as they renew their contracts.
OpenAI made a similar pricing change in April. The Codex rate card [ https://substack.com/redirect/5edb7cfb-2c3a-4e20-9d70-0679b848a81b?j=eyJ1IjoiOGZ6aG43In0.MEdLiOcZRUc_N3oL6SgEUFCyFYN9tX8izo2S8jR1GNw ] (Internet Archive copy [ https://substack.com/redirect/7577271d-117e-4b6f-9cdf-eaca655f1076?j=eyJ1IjoiOGZ6aG43In0.MEdLiOcZRUc_N3oL6SgEUFCyFYN9tX8izo2S8jR1GNw ]) currently says:
Note: On April 2, 2026, we updated Codex pricing to align with API token usage, instead of per-message pricing. This change was applicable to new and existing Plus, Pro, ChatGPT Business and new ChatGPT Enterprise plans.
On April 23, 2026, we made this update for all existing ChatGPT Enterprise plans as well, inclusive of Edu, Health, Gov, and ChatGPT for Teachers.
It’s a little harder to decode as they quote prices in “credits”, but as far as I can tell those credit costs are an exact match for the API token costs listed for those models.
All of which is to say that as of April 2026 the “Enterprise” cost for both OpenAI Codex and Anthropic Claude Code/Cowork is the same as the listed API price.
GPT-5.5 (released April 23rd) is 2x the API price of GPT-5.4. Opus 4.7 (April 16th) is around 1.4x [ https://substack.com/redirect/d31eaa41-a506-4125-91c8-58e04418278c?j=eyJ1IjoiOGZ6aG43In0.MEdLiOcZRUc_N3oL6SgEUFCyFYN9tX8izo2S8jR1GNw ] the price of Opus 4.6 when you take their new tokenizer into account.
So April saw both leading model companies release new frontier models with a higher API price, and both companies now have measures to lock their enterprise customers (who tend to sign year-long deals) at those API prices, not the previous extreme discounts.
I think they’ve found product-market fit
Why these sudden aggressive moves on pricing? Both Anthropic and OpenAI are planning to IPO, but I suspect there’s a more important factor here: I think they’ve finally found product-market fit, with the coding/general-purpose agent products embodied by Claude Code/Cowork and Codex.
Tools like ChatGPT are wildly popular, but that wild popularity has been difficult to turn into revenue. In February OpenAI boasted [ https://substack.com/redirect/87aee75b-116a-4784-a659-e4922119901a?j=eyJ1IjoiOGZ6aG43In0.MEdLiOcZRUc_N3oL6SgEUFCyFYN9tX8izo2S8jR1GNw ] more than 900 million weekly active users for ChatGPT, but only 50 million - 5.6% of that - were paying consumer subscribers.
Charging $10-$20/month per user is an OK business, but you’d need 1-2 billion subscribers sticking around for four years to cover $1 trillion in infrastructure [ https://substack.com/redirect/d75ecf15-17f2-4206-983d-5a11fa054abf?j=eyJ1IjoiOGZ6aG43In0.MEdLiOcZRUc_N3oL6SgEUFCyFYN9tX8izo2S8jR1GNw ].
Companies spending $200+/month/user will get you there a whole lot faster - and as noted above, as a power-user I’m at ~$1,000/month in API costs per vendor already.
Coding agents really did change everything. These are tools which burn vastly more tokens, but are also quickly becoming daily drivers for the work carried out by extremely well-compensated professionals. Right now that’s still mostly software engineers, but a coding agent is a tool that can automate anything you can do by typing commands into a computer... so they are clearly applicable to a much wider set of skilled knowledge workers.

## Phill Agnew — This viral prank is a warning to all AI gurus | Nudge Newsletter

_From: `[email]` · 2026-05-29T09:01:59+00:00_

********************
The AI Contradiction
********************

​Read online ( https://a7046da1.click.kit-mail3.com/68ukw58k64c8h58w69wfohp4glwm7h9h7orl5/8ghqhohovqxx84bk/aHR0cHM6Ly9udWRnZS5raXQuY29tL3Byb2ZpbGU= )​

I just generated an image in the style of Monet using AI.

Have a look, and think about what makes this inferior to a real Monet painting.

Made with AI*
A few weeks back, X user "SHLOMS" did the same.

SHLOM's post on X.
1,300 people responded. Most said this AI art was pure crap.
​
They said it lacked "coherent composition".
​
The colours were an "incoherent muddle".
​
Some said it was "trying too hard".
​
Others called it "obvious AI slop".

Replies to "SHLOMS" included "it's garbage". Credit to Rundown AI for the image.
​

But there's a problem...

This Monet painting is real.
​

I'll be honest. My gut reaction to the screenshot is the same. I immediately think it's slop. I try to spot flaws and think the colours are dull.
​
Because all of us do.
​
We follow what Morales¹ called an 'effort heuristic'. In other words, if something took two seconds to generate, we'll hate it. If it took 15 years of craft to perfect, we'll love it.
​
In her 2005 study, 46 people hired a real estate agent.
​
The agent reviewed their preferences and put together a personalised list of 10 apartments.
​
However, 23 of the participants were told the agent:
​
​"Did everything manually and spent 9 hours building the list." ​
​
The other 23 were told:
​
​"The agent used a computer program, spending only 1 hour on the list."

​
​
In reality, the houses on both lists were identical.
​
But perception was swayed by the perceived effort.
​
Those who were told the list took 9 hours to create rated the houses 30.5% higher.

​
​
We use effort as a proxy to measure quality. Especially when quality is hard to measure.
​
So when 6.8 million people saw a real Monet but thought it was created using AI, they immediately called it slop.

This presents a contradiction.

We're repeatedly told by AI-peddlers that to compete, we need to embrace AI.

But the Morales study shows the opposite.

If we use AI (or even if people think we use AI), people will feel a urge to hate our work.

Dave Harland calls this 'Death By Sepia' ( https://a7046da1.click.kit-mail3.com/68ukw58k64c8h58w69wfohp4glwm7h9h7orl5/vqh3hrho7edd52hg/aHR0cHM6Ly9kYXNoYm9hcmQubWFpbGVybGl0ZS5jb20vZm9ybXMvODkwNDYvNTk0MzU1MDY3NDI1OTI4Mzkvc2hhcmU= )​

Taken from Dave's "The Word" newsletter (sign up here ( https://a7046da1.click.kit-mail3.com/68ukw58k64c8h58w69wfohp4glwm7h9h7orl5/vqh3hrho7edd52hg/aHR0cHM6Ly9kYXNoYm9hcmQubWFpbGVybGl0ZS5jb20vZm9ybXMvODkwNDYvNTk0MzU1MDY3NDI1OTI4Mzkvc2hhcmU= )).
The landlord at the Bluebell might think this is infinitely better than a bog-standard blackboard sign.

They might say, "It's colourful! Stands out! It includes all of our menu! (Even a goblet of wine)."

But most people will see it and recognise that off-sepia tone as AI.

And as we've seen with Monet, once people think something is AI, they'll hate it.

buy?” The useful idea here is token-to-outcome tracking: cost per
resolved ticket, processed claim, reviewed contract, avoided hire, or
dollar of revenue moved. For founders selling AI into companies, usage
is not enough. The buyer will soon want proof that inference spend
turns into work that matters.

adaptable intelligence, creating a need for robust AI harness systems.

effectively managing these elements will dominate the emerging
competitive landscape in software.

# Dispatches from Press Publish LA: The Hollywood Creator Summit

View image: (https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/9662c77a-b7be-49e9-918e-60e6303f4caa/0529_Article_Photo_2__1_.png?t=1780070775)
Caption: (Left to right) Emmy award-winning creator journalist Johnny Harris, Beast Industries head of talent Kara McCloud, and _Challenge Accepted_ host Michelle Khare speak on the Main Stage at Press Publish LA / Photography by Jesse Leon

Yesterday, we gathered almost 700 creators, operators, and industry professionals on the Fox lot for our second Press Publish summit—this time, focused on the convergence of Hollywood and the creator economy.

Creators flew in from Amsterdam, Switzerland, and Hong Kong. The day's surprises included a marching band, a motorcycle stunt man, and an appearance from film and game creator Markiplier. But the best part? The conversations that happened in between. **Here are some of the top quotes and learnings from the day** →

**“I enter YouTube coming from a doubtful place and I’m addicted to overcoming that doubt,”** our surprise guest [Markiplier](https://www.instagram.com/p/DY5UYP3yz3B/) said on the main stage. He shared that his movie _Iron Lung_ made $52M in over 4,200 theaters with a budget of just under $5M. _Iron Lung_ releases on YouTube today.

**“I can’t teach someone to care about the work that they’re doing, but I can teach YouTube,” **Beast Industries head of talent Kara McCloud said. As hire #12 on the team (which now has 780+ employees), McCloud saw there was no talent incubator in the creator economy. So she set out to make Beast Industries the starting point for young professionals in the creator world—and the result was alumni like [Anthpo](https://www.instagram.com/anthpo/) and [Ernesto Perez](https://www.linkedin.com/in/ernestoperezjr/), to name a few.

**“YouTube is a volume game,”** creator journalist Johnny Harris said [on stage](https://www.instagram.com/p/DY5rwNtRQQK/?hl=en) (less than 24 hours after winning an Emmy in NY). For years, Harris focused on becoming reliable for his audience, so they would stick around when he pivoted to a project that required more planning—like his new show _The Human Element_. The difference between a YouTube video and a show, according to Harris?

“I started to put more time in development,” Harris said. “I think this show is a more intentional vision that underpins it.” 

**“Content needs to be timely or timeless,”** TBPN co-founder John Coogan said. On stage, Coogan and co-founder Jordi Hays shared top lessons from turning their niche livestream into a [nine-figure exit](https://techcrunch.com/2026/04/02/openai-acquires-tbpn-the-buzzy-founder-led-business-talk-show/). They said choosing either end of the [content barbell](https://www.instagram.com/p/DY6AyYcRRKw/) (long-form or daily posting) is the way you can win—because if you’re timely but only post once a week, there’s someone who is publishing once a day and getting better faster. 

**Formatting is world-building.** Michelle Khare’s seven marathons series went through several iterations before [debuting in three parts](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3zDt-QeJIw4&list=PLGjBhEbq3-8w5qyaFQE8gwYSpoh1C-9G_). The single 90-minute cut lost the plot lines about her fellow runners (the emotional core of the series), and a seven-part version of the series was too loose. Even within the long-form format, Khare had to experiment to find what worked for the specific story she was telling. 

**But that’s just a taste:** We’ll be back on Monday with even more learnings, including more insight on the future of indie film distribution from Markiplier. Session recaps from our partner, Google Gemini, are coming soon.

* FCS and YMH will split ownership of the productions. 

* Fox will also bring its advertising sales to YMH’s existing podcast network, which has 25+ shows with a collective 2 million followers.

**What makes this creator deal different: **Fox Creator Studios is less focused on distribution—not licensing shows or putting them on Fox platforms. Instead, the projects with Segura and YMH will live across YMH’s existing platforms, leaning into its community and scaling direct-to-consumer relationships.

"We're hyper-focused on creators doubling down on channels that work for them," said Billy Parks, Head of FCS, told us in a call previewing the announcement.

The rise of interest media continues to get bigger and bigger. And it’s gotten to the point where it’s not something you can ignore. It’s something you should strategize around. It’s a huge opportunity if you build the right team or infrastructure to take advantage of it.

**_Why?_**

From the beginning of the social era, growing a following was very hard. Of course, there was the anomaly. But that wasn’t the majority, and every small or new account was at a big disadvantage with a big road ahead of them. And that’s why so many brands backed out of organic. They weren’t willing to build a car that made it down the road.

_**But here’s the opportunity.**_

An account that has 10 million followers and an account that has 0 followers can both get 10M views tomorrow.

**Read that again.**

And I know because we’ve seen it happen 100 hundreds of times with Cut30 and hundreds of times with brands we work with. We’ll make a video around a very specific topic like “leather making,” and it’ll get hundreds of thousands of views in 24 hours, and it’ll come from a small account.

_**Why and how does that happen?**_

Because…

## Interest Is The Distribution

View image: (https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/d6474cf5-2d4d-4651-83b3-30a93f4df2dc/The_Rise_Of_Interest_Media-01__1_.jpg?t=1780004320)
Caption: 

In the past, a follower account meant everything. Every follow was a physical pipe between two accounts that allowed you to publish a piece of content and send it straight through the pipe to the person on the other side.

More followers meant more pipes.

And more pipes meant more reach.

**Now, pipes are created based on two factors:**

1. The topic (who it’s for)

2. The data (how well it performs)

So, if someone loves trail running and you create trail running content, then the algo will recognize the alignment and route your content through a new pipe that didn’t exist for them.

And not because they follow you.

**But because the interest match exists. That connection is the distribution.**

View image: (https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/c59eef59-9184-4c91-9ecb-53d0eaec9817/The_Rise_Of_Interest_Media-02__1_.jpg?t=1780004303)
Caption: 

This changes what an “audience” means.

You’re not just building a following anymore.

**You’re building a body of content that’s positioned inside an interest cluster.**

And anyone who enters that cluster from now until the algo changes is a potential viewer.

So, your reach isn't capped by a follower count anymore but is bounded only by how many people share that interest.

The stronger the signal, the more precisely the algorithm can find the right people. Vague content creates vague distribution. Specific content creates specific, qualified distribution.

## Specificity is The Signal

If I needed to mail something to someone in Florida, I would never put “somewhere in Florida” as the address.

I would obviously put an address like:

12345 Parker Ln,
Miami, FL 33128

So, the exact thing I want delivered gets delivered.

Specificity in content now acts like an address getting routed to the exact person interested in that thing.

And most brands think going specific means shrinking their potential audience.

No.

That specificity is data. And concentrates it on people who will be obsessed with the content.

Once I find winning ads in my testing campaign, I take two actions.

→ Duplicate them into the scaling campaign. 

I have a new ad set waiting there with a min spend limit so I can force spend onto those newer winners instead of letting Meta dump everything into the old historical winners.

→ Scale it up. 

I'll typically increase the budget by 20-30% every day or so as long as the CPA holds up.

The winners also stay running in the testing campaign. Some ads work better at lower spend so I keep them alive in the ABO at their sweet spot while the duplicate scales in the CBO.

So it's not either or. Duplicate to scaling, scale the budget gradually, and leave the original running where it already works.

## @benradack
My client's creative testing campaign is 50% of their account budget.

Here's why.

Sometimes ads that work in your ABO testing ad sets don't work in your scaling campaign. Either Meta doesn't favor them or they only perform at smaller spends.

So I scale those winners up inside the ABO instead of forcing them into scaling. Over time my testing campaign ends up with a lot of profitable ad sets running at their natural ceiling.

That's how it grows to 50% of the budget.

Important distinction though.

I'm not allocating half my budget to new tests. I'm allocating half my budget to a campaign that contains both proven testing ad sets AND new tests.

If I gave half my budget to brand new untested ads and most failed, I'd be hurting the account.

The new tests inside that campaign are a small slice. The bulk of the spend is going to ad sets that have already proven themselves and are scaling at their sweet spot.

The testing campaign isn't just for testing anymore. It's also where ads live that work better at lower budgets.

Something I keep noticing when I study native ad funnels that have been running for 12+ months:

The advertorials that survive are the ones that could stand alone as articles.

The product recommendation at the end just feels like the logical conclusion.

Write it that way.

## @advertising_jan
If you're new here, a quick overview of what native advertising actually is.

Native ads are the "recommended content" links you see at the bottom of news articles on sites like CNN, Fox News, Daily Mail.

They're served by platforms like Taboola and Outbrain.

They look like editorial content, not ads.

The reader arrives from a news article. They're in reading mode, not shopping mode.

That's why a direct link to a product page almost never works.

You need an advertorial in between. An 800-word article that earns trust, explains the problem, introduces a solution, and then recommends the product.

The reader arrives cold. They leave warm.

That's the whole model.

It's the most underrated ad channel in ecom right now.

Make the benefit visible: things that work but stay invisible don't build trust. If the payoff isn't felt on screen, it doesn't register. Worth auditing whether any of your pain points or product benefits are still living in the abstract.

People want to feel liked back. Hank frames it as: the content people are starving for is competence that also seems to care about them. That's also a near-perfect brief for brand voice. Are you signalling that you see your audience, or just targeting them?

Mostly a US lens right now, but likely to trickle down into online (thus, global) discourses

## @iamshackelford
Everyone obsesses over LTV.

But LTV is a lagging indicator. By the time you can measure it cleanly, the decisions that created it are 12 months old.

The leading indicator nobody talks about?

Days between order 1 and order 2.

I've looked at hundreds of brand dashboards. The healthiest ones aren't the ones with the biggest repeat rate. They're the ones with the shortest gap.

A customer who comes back in 25 days is worth 3-4x a customer who comes back in 75 days.
Same product. Same AOV. Different velocity.

Because velocity compounds.

Buy every 30 days = 12 orders a year. Buy every 60 days = 6 orders a year. Buy every 90 days = 4 orders a year.

Same customer. Same loyalty. Wildly different business.

So the real question isn't "how do I get more repeat customers."

It's "how do I shorten the gap."

Here's what's working right now:

Step 1: Pull your actual median days-between-orders. Not your gut. The number.

Step 2: Identify the customers sitting at 1.5x that number. They're the leak.

Step 3: Build one flow. Trigger it 7-10 days before their expected reorder date. Two CTAs: → "Reorder in one click" → "See what's new"

That's it. No 14-email nurture sequence. No win-back campaign with three discount tiers.

The brands with the best retention aren't the ones with the most sophisticated email program. They're the ones easiest to buy from a second time.

## @theecommike
numbers going up means you're making progress

every teacher told you this
every parent celebrated it

your entire life was graded on whether the number moved in the right direction

and then you build a real business and realise the number that's going up is sometimes the most dangerous thing in the room

this month my store did 729,000 sessions

up 13% from last month

and revenue came in at $5.95 million

down 19%

and the first thing most people would do with that information is panic

find more traffic, push more budget, test new audiences, get the sessions number higher

because the sessions are going up so that must be the lever

it isn't

i saw what was happening three weeks before the revenue moved

one creative carrying a significant portion of account revenue started showing early fatigue signals

thumb stop rate trending down across three consecutive days

frequency climbing on the audiences that had been converting hardest

hook rate holding but watch time dropping

the creative was still running, still spending, still bringing sessions in

but it was bringing in the wrong sessions

people who clicked out of mild curiosity instead of people who clicked because something in the ad spoke directly to their situation

we pulled it, rebuilt the brief from scratch around a different psychological angle, had new creatives in testing within a week

$5.95 million during a transition month where the engine was being rebuilt mid-flight is not a loss

it's what a store looks

## @cjslattery
We cut $2,200 a month off our software stack last quarter and didn't lose a single capability. Most of what we canceled were API wrappers charging us for data we already owned.

Strip away the marketing, and a lot of DTC SaaS tools are just a connection to an ad platform's API that reformats data you can already pull yourself.

Some of them run $2k+/month and climb as you add clients. For too long, software has been operating at 80% gross margins with marginal cost of scale.

So I got relentless about our stack. Every quarter and before any renewal, we run it through three questions:

1. Are people on the team actually using this?
2. Is it expensive enough to deserve real scrutiny?
3. Are we paying for two tools that do the same job?

Anything that can't clear those gets cut.

There's a good chance a similar number is hiding in your stack. If you want a second set of eyes on what's actually worth keeping, I'd be happy to take a look.

At the time, I was living in a $475/mo room in a rundown building in Bed Stuy, where I didn't have access to a bathroom. As a result, I lost that room and when I got out of the hospital, my sister allowed me 2 weeks to find a new place to live before I was out on the street.  

My housing had been sporadic since my mother got evicted right after my 18th birthday, and I was forced to live on my own. I remember working at a bakery in the West Village and lived in Washington Heights, and I'd walk to and from work because I couldn't afford the subway fare. 

On Christmas Eve 2009, I took the $127 I had saved and started Taikun. It was a web hosting company. I bought the domain name, I got a reseller hosting license, and I setup WHM and a website. items.content: Your FBA Margins Are Bleeding. Here's Why You Can't See It. Andy Jassy said it plainly on the Q1 2026 earnings call: the inventory stockpiling that brands did ahead of tariffs is burned through. The buffer is gone. Combined with a 3.5% increase in FBA fees that took effect in April, sellers are now operating in a margin environment that is meaningfully worse than it was six months ago, and will feel it in Q2 P&Ls.This matters beyond Amazon. For DTC brands that run multi-channel operations, selling on Shopify, selling on Amazon, running paid social and search, the hidden danger is that margin compression on FBA SKUs is invisible in blended reporting. Your overall ROAS looks acceptable. Your total revenue is growing. But three or four high-volume SKUs are quietly destroying your contribution margin, and your dashboard isn't built to show you that.Why Do Blended Metrics Hide Margin Compression?Here's how the compression sneaks up on you: you track blended ROAS across your Meta and Google spend. That ROAS is calculated against total revenue, including Amazon revenue that came from customers who saw your DTC ads and then bought on Amazon anyway. The ad platform gets credit. The FBA fee increase is buried in your operations line. The connection between media spend and actual margin never gets made.Across the 230+ brands we track through Statlas, we see this pattern constantly. Customer acquisition cost on Meta has risen 31% since early 2024, from $40.27 to $52.86. Average order value has moved barely at all: $124.85 to $125.85.
